newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-MMC warns on Australia car industry.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-MMC warns on Australia car industry.

text.p: Mitsubishi Motors Australia Ltd (MMAL) said on Tuesday the Australian automotive industry would not survive through to 2010 if the Australian government accepted a proposal to cut tariffs to five percent by 2004.

"We believe (if the government adopts the Productivity Commission proposal) it is a matter of when, not if the industry ceases," Mitsubishi managing director Mike Quinn told a news conference. Quinn said the benefits of a tariff reduction from 15 percent in 2000 to five percent in 2004 were very small.
"The risk is enormous, the risk is that you would lose the industry and lose 100,000 jobs," Quinn said after addressing the commission at a public hearing in Adelaide.
"So what politician could rightly take that decision?"

Asked whether Mitsubishi would close down its operations immediately if the proposal were adopted, Quinn said it would make its decision, like other locally based car manufacturers, at the convenient time but would "not be running ahead of the others in either direction".
Each company would make its decision to suit its model, investment and marketing cycles, he said, but added a warning.
"Quite honestly as one pulls out, to me it will have an effect of bringing along other problems within the industry and hasten along the downfall of it," he said.
Quinn said he did not believe the Productivity Commission was likely to dramatically change its position on tariffs, and so it was up to the government to make a sensible decision.

"At present we are like people in a mile race and we have gone out sprinting for the first lap and nobody else is doing anything," he said referring to the pace of tariff cuts in Australia compared to other nations.
Quinn later said Mitsubishi had experienced another tough year in 1996, but would not reveal further details ahead of the publication of annual results in April or May.
"It needs improving from where we are," he said.
Quinn said Mitsubishi expected to achieve A$620 million in export revenue in 1997.
Mitsubishi, sensitive to the Japanese yen and under pressure from imports, posted a net loss of A$43 million in calendar 1995, compared to A$10.6 million net profit in 1994.

Australia's automotive industry has undergone radical restructuring over the last decade, with a reduction in tariffs from 52.5 percent in 1985 to 22.5 percent now and production down from 377,000 units in 1985 to around 323,000 in 1996.
In that time, the number of manufacturers has dropped from five to four -- Mitsubishi and units of Ford Motor Co, General MOtors Corp and Toyota Motor Corp.

Official figures show Australian new vehicle sales rose 1.2 percent to 650,000 units in 1996 from 1995 but the industry expects sales to drop three percent in 1997, under further pressure from cheap imports particularly from Korea.
Quinn said imports made up 57 percent of new sales in Australia in January 1997.
